Several threads led to the title of this entry. One thread was from thinking about Ulrich's take on critical systems thinking; one way to frame the systemology/systems thinking debate is the question of whether systems are discovered or invented, which places the debate in the classical physis/nomos division. Rousseau's systemology includes both "science" and "engineering" as components of the larger framework, which can be generalized as "discovery" or "invention".

Another thread was Metzger's doctoral thesis on "semeiotic realism", which argued against Deely's interpretation that Peirce was directly influenced by the Latin debate over *signum*. I only read the first 30 pages or so, so I'm willing to hear out the argument, but if there is a difference between Peirce and Pointsot, is it clear that Peirce's solution is superior? Poinsot's argument that the category of relation transcends the division between physis and nomos.

Another thread was today's Gray Area podcast titled (*The People Who Want AI to Replace Us*)[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b30d7FR8YP0]. Note the podcast title differs from the YouTube title of *Should we let humans go extinct*. The hosts pushed back on the successionist model (i.e. that AI will replace humanity) with the notion of humanism, but advocated for including all life within the concern of humanism. But successionism is grounded in an extreme form of rationalism, which says that intelligence is the single greatest value and that utilitarianism necessarily embraces this extreme rationalism (I'm not sure I agree, but there is a thread). The whole debate struck me as embracing "organicism" as the only model of self-organization and the quasi-religious worship of evolution. I believe it was M.A. Jackson that proposed the "polis" as another model of self-organization, which I'd like to follow up on.

These thoughts crystallized around the question "is mathematics invented or discovered" that I posed to Gemini, which I followed up with "mathematics discovered invented physis nomos". Gemini had a pretty good answer in terms of historical background but settled for "a mixture of both". So then I followed up with:

> Can you explain how John Locke's notion of semiotics was intended to transcend the physis/nomos duality and did he believe that mathematics was a branch of semiotics?

Gemini responded that Locke did not propose semiotics as an answer to the physis/nomos debate but also that Locke proposed that ideas were signs and that they served as a bridge between "physica"  and "practica" (Locke didn't use the term *nomos*). Lock concluded that logic and mathematics were both branches of semiotics since they both studied "ideas in the mind". Locke also argued that mathematics allowed access to "absolute certainty" since "mathematical ideas are completely generated by the mind".

I followed up with the following question:

> John Deely considered Locke a philosopher in the way of ideas, and contrasted his semiotics with his contemporary John Poinsot. Can you explain Deely's argument on how Poinsot's theory of signs differs from Locke's?

Gemini answered:

> According to Deely, the defining difference between Locke and Poinsot lies in how they defined the relationship between a representation and a sign.

>  Locke argued that the immediate objects of human knowledge are internal "ideas". For Locke, an idea is an internal representation that stands in front of the mind like a picture or a mirror image of the outside world. Deely points out that this inevitably leads to solipsism or idealism. If we only look at our internal ideas, we can never prove that they accurately match the real, physical world outside.

> Poinsot made a radical, foundational distinction: all signs involve representation, but not all representations are signs. A representation merely presents an object to a power (like a mirror reflecting light), but a sign connects three separate things in a triadic relation. In Poinsot's framework, a relation is unique because its essential being (esse) is purely "inter-subjective" — it exists between things, rather than inside a thing. Poinsot noted that a relation does not care whether its terms are real or imaginary.

Although Poinsot's approach argues for relational realism, it doesn't really solve the problem of how these relations exist in reality. Peirce naturalizes the notion of relation into the notion of habit. Habit's can be natural (like a law of physics) or conventional (like a belief). Peirce also argues that habits arise through evolution rather than being created, so habit's themselves are neither simply invented or simply discovered.

Peirce bases his philosophical concept of habit on a mathematical analysis of the conditional. Belucci argued that Peirce developed this concept from the medieval doctrine of "consequentiae". According to Bellucci, 

> But for Peirce an argument is always equivalent or reducible to a conditional proposition, and thus the relation of illation can always be expressed in a conditional in which the premise is the antecedent and the conclusion the consequent.

Peirce distinguishes between material and formal principles of reasoning, and seeks to find the minimal set of formal/logical principles that cannot be made a premise of an argument. A "leading principle" is a rule in a syllogism. It is a combination of matter and form. Once all matter is transferred to the premises, what remains is a "logical principle" (shouldn't this be a formal principle?). It has achieved "a maximum degree of abstractness". Stjernfelt called this strategy "blocking evil infinities". The trigger is that attempting to remove matter from a formal principle leads to an infinite regress. 

The claim is that all arguments can be expressed as a conditional proposition for which the premises are the antecedent, the conclusion the consequent, and the link between them the "consequentiae". 

> We saw that Peirce praises Tartaretus’ definition of the consequentia as habitudo or principle of inference: ‘more properly, the consequentia was the leading principle’.

In a footnote on p. 20, Bellucci states:

> Peirce’s subsequent move, which I do not have space to discuss here, was to classify arguments on the basis of their logical leading principles. According to Peirce, arguments are either hypotheses (later: abductions), inductions, or deductions, each kind having its own characteristic logical principle, which Peirce preferred to express in semiotic terms: in hypothesis, induction, and deduction the premises are an icon, an index, and a symbol of the conclusion, respectively. See W 1.186-188, W 2.58; see also Bellucci 2014 and Bellucci 2015a.
